title: Prenatal exposure to cigarette smoke induces diet- and sex-dependent dyslipidemia and weight gain in adult murine offspring.
ehr_evidence: We exposed B6C3F1 mice (via whole-body inhalation) to either filtered air or mainstream cigarette smoke (MCS, at a particle concentration of 15 mg/m3) from gestational day 4 to parturition; plasma lipid parameters, lipoprotein subclass particle numbers and sizes, and total antioxidant capacities were measured.
summary: In a controlled experimental mouse study, B6C3F1 offspring prenatally exposed to mainstream cigarette smoke via whole-body inhalation developed sex- and diet-dependent increases in body weight and dyslipidemia in adulthood.
key_findings: Adult female mice prenatally exposed to MCS and fed a normal diet weighed significantly more than air-exposed counterparts (p < 0.05) with no difference in male body weight on normal diet.
When fed a high-fat diet for 2 weeks, male offspring prenatally exposed to MCS gained substantially more weight than sex-matched air-exposed counterparts (p < 0.05).
Only triglyceride (TRI) levels were significantly altered (decreased by 31%) in dams after direct MCS inhalation compared with air-exposed counterparts.

Prenatal MCS exposure significantly increased total LDL particle concentration (air vs. MCS, 5.9 ± 5.9 vs. 56.6 ± 3.0 nmol/L) and large LDL particle concentration (4.3 ± 4.3 vs. 42.4 ± 4.2 nmol/L) in adult female offspring.
MCS exposure had no effect on HDL or VLDL and chylomicron particle concentrations in female offspring, and no differences in particle concentrations or size in male offspring.
No significant differences were observed between air- and smoke-exposed groups in total antioxidant capacity (TAC) in either sex.
Female offspring exposed to MCS on a normal diet showed significant increases in plasma HDL, LDL, and total protein levels; these effects were no longer visible in the HFD-fed group.
captured_features: NMR lipoprotein subclass particle numbers and sizes (HDL, LDL, VLDL)
population: B6C3F1 mice exposed in utero to cigarette smoke, assessed through gestation to adult offspring at 13-14 weeks of age
limitations: Protein content differed between the normal chow and high-fat diets, so observed changes may be partly attributable to dietary calorie/protein differences.
Small sample sizes in some analyses (e.g., n = 3 for NMR HDL particle concentration comparisons).
Mouse exposure model reflects only the first two trimesters of human gestation.
The specific underlying mechanism(s) by which prenatal MCS exposure caused the observed changes remains unknown.
